claim: Convergence criteria tested at application, "not enforced afterwards"

edits.old: Before a country can adopt the euro it must meet convergence criteria written into the EU Treaty. The idea is that economies sharing one interest rate should already look alike: low inflation, sound public finances, a stable exchange rate and long-term interest rates close to the best performers. The criteria are tested when a country applies for membership, not enforced afterwards, which is one reason the tests are strict.
edits.new: Before a country can adopt the euro it must meet convergence criteria written into the EU Treaty. The idea is that economies sharing one interest rate should already look alike: low inflation, sound public finances, a stable exchange rate and long-term interest rates close to the best performers. The criteria are tested before a country is allowed in; once it has joined it can no longer devalue or set its own interest rate, which is one reason the entry tests are strict.

note: "Not enforced afterwards" is wrong: the 3% deficit and 60% debt reference values keep applying to members through EU fiscal rules. Example thresholds (1.5 pp, 3%, 60%, 2 years, 2 pp) all confirmed.

claim: Managed float: basket reference, daily central parity and band; 1994 unification; 2005 reform; band 0.3% to 0.5% in 2007

edits.old: A managed floating exchange rate lets the currency move with market supply and demand inside limits set by the central bank. China's version references a basket of currencies rather than the U.S. dollar alone, and the central bank publishes a daily central parity around which trading may move within a band. It is neither a hard peg nor a free float.
edits.new: A managed floating exchange rate lets the currency move with market supply and demand inside limits set by the central bank. China's version references a basket of currencies rather than the U.S. dollar alone, and a daily central parity is set around which trading may move within a band. It is neither a hard peg nor a free float.

note: Dates and bands confirmed. The parity is announced through the interbank market system, not published by the central bank itself; neutral wording used. Example is correctly historical (band widened again after 2007).

claim: 9 largest US banks 176% of capital by 1982; lost decade; Brady plan forgave $61bn (~one-third) 1989-94; regulators vetted banks

edits.old: A debt crisis becomes a lost decade when the cure, austerity to keep paying, chokes growth for years. Debt reduction breaks the cycle by writing part of the debt off in exchange for new bonds the borrower can service. Lenders accept a loss because a smaller debt that gets paid is worth more than a larger one that does not. Regulators first had to be sure the banks could absorb the write-offs.
edits.new: A debt crisis becomes a lost decade when the cure, austerity to keep paying, chokes growth for years. Debt reduction breaks the cycle by writing part of the debt off in exchange for new bonds the borrower can service. Lenders accept a loss because a smaller debt that gets paid is worth more than a larger one that does not. Banks first had to set aside enough loss reserves to absorb the write-offs.

note: Example figures confirmed. The essay says regulators let banks delay recognizing losses, while banks (Citibank first, 1987) built loss provisions; the regulator sentence was unsupported.

claim: Peg fixes rate to the dollar; Thailand devalued July 2, 1997; spread through Dec 1998; $118bn mobilized for 3 countries

edits.old: A currency peg fixes the exchange rate to the dollar. It invites firms and banks to borrow in dollars, often short term, because the rate seems guaranteed. If foreign lenders lose confidence and pull out, the central bank runs short of reserves and the peg breaks. The currency falls, and every dollar debt suddenly costs far more in local money, pushing borrowers into insolvency.
edits.new: A currency peg fixes the exchange rate to another currency, often the U.S. dollar. It invites firms and banks to borrow in dollars, often short term, because the rate seems guaranteed. If foreign lenders lose confidence and pull out, the central bank runs short of reserves and the peg breaks. The currency falls, and every dollar debt suddenly costs far more in local money, pushing borrowers into insolvency.

note: Example facts confirmed. A peg is not by definition to the dollar; general definition corrected.
